disease_label_per_paper: Neurobrucellosis with transient ischemic attack, vasculopathic changes, intracerebral granulomas and basal ganglia infarction
presentation_summary: Previously healthy 17-year-old male had a transient episode of left arm weakness, hypoesthesia, speech disturbance, and imbalance, followed 2 weeks later by worsening headache, double vision, nausea, vomiting, and fever.
Admission exam showed fever 38 degC, doubtful neck stiffness, and left abducens nerve paralysis; initial systemic exam was otherwise nonspecific.
Initial labs showed WBC 5.9 x10^9/L with 55% neutrophils and 45% lymphocytes, ESR 2 mm/h, CRP 3.0 mg/dL, and normal blood chemistry/liver enzymes.
Initial CSF showed 104 cells/uL with 90% lymphocytes, protein 250 mg/dL, glucose 22 mg/dL, and concurrent blood glucose 72 mg/dL; early Brucella tests and cultures were negative.

On hospital day 30 he developed generalized tonic-clonic seizures; on day 31 he had fever 38.2 degC, neck stiffness, facial paralysis, left hemiparesis, MRI evidence of vasculitis/infarcts/granuloma, and repeat CSF pleocytosis. Serum and CSF Rose-Bengal, STA, and ELISA IgM/IgG became positive.

actual_treatment: initial empiric tuberculosis meningitis therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and prednisolone
after neurobrucellosis diagnosis: TMP/SMX 160/800 mg three times daily

outcome.clinical_course: Fever disappeared 10 days after brucellosis therapy; symptoms improved completely by 6 months; no complaints at 3-year follow-up.
outcome.source_text_value: Other signs and symptoms improved completely at the end of the sixth month of therapy

quality_warnings: Brucella-specific serology and culture results are placed in confirmatory_findings. CSF cell count, protein, glucose, neurologic deficits, and fever are ordinary observations because they are presentation/pathophysiology measurements rather than organism confirmation.
The paper reports CSF cells as cells/mL in prose; stored as cells/uL to match project CSF axis convention and the article's own table-style clinical meaning.
